Title: Венгрию ждут выборы. Закончится ли 15-летнее правление Виктора Орбана?

Summary: 
Hungary is approaching its 2026 parliamentary elections amid escalating tensions with Brussels, energy instability, and intense domestic political competition. The ruling party Fidesz-KDNP, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, has held power for 15 years and is seeking re-election, though its position has weakened. According to research by the independent Hungarian Institute for Political Studies (Policy Solutions), public confidence in Orbán’s government has declined, with growing criticism of Hungary’s international standing and EU fund freezes attributed to Orbán’s administration. A majority of Hungarians now view opposition leader Péter Márki-Zay of the Tisza party as a more suitable candidate than Orbán, with support for Márki-Zay rising even among undecided voters. Orbán’s campaign focuses on maintaining neutrality in the Ukraine conflict, warning that pro-Bruce-loyal candidates would drag Hungary into war. However, public fear of war has decreased: in 2023, 59% feared Hungary’s involvement; by autumn 2025, this dropped to 46%, and further to 43% by late 2025. Another key issue is opposition to Ukraine’s EU accession, with 64% of Hungarians opposing it and only 31% supporting it by 2025. Orbán has leveraged this sentiment, aligning with farmers’ protests against EU subsidies. The Tisza party, a pro-European liberal force, criticizes Orbán’s foreign policy, especially ties with Russia, China, and Turkey, and promotes cooperation with the EU and Ursula von der Leyen. Tisza has gained popularity due to its competence narrative and anti-corruption stance, with 58% of respondents believing it is more capable than Fidesz in handling state affairs. The Democratic Coalition (DK), led by Klára Dobrev, is weaker but may coordinate with Tisza. The far-right 'Our Homeland' (Mi Hazánk), led by László Tóthkács, has grown steadily, gaining nearly 7% in the 2024 European Parliament elections, advocating for Hungarian rights in Transcarpathia and promoting anti-immigrant, anti-Islamic, and anti-Semitic views. Orbán’s government has tightened media control through a state oversight body targeting foreign-funded outlets, drawing criticism from the EU for restricting press freedom. The opposition uses this to discredit Orbán. Despite Orbán’s strong base of around two million voters, political analysts like Zoltán Kiseli suggest this is insufficient for victory. The outcome will shape Hungary’s future: a Fidesz win would maintain resistance to Ukraine’s EU integration and skepticism toward EU-led escalation; a Tisza victory would align Hungary more closely with EU pro-Ukraine policies. Orbán’s foreign policy, including close ties with U.S. figures like Donald Trump and JD Vance, suggests a strategic positioning in a shifting global order, though he avoids explicitly defining it.

Title: BALKAN BLOG: Beyond Hungary, elections in Bulgaria and Slovenia to shape eastern EU’s political map

In Bulgaria, political fragmentation and fatigue persist amid its eighth parliamentary election in five years. A coalition associated with former president Rumen Radev is projected to lead, though Radev has not formally launched a party. Radev, once aligned with reformist CC-DB, has shifted toward a ‘non-involvement’ stance on the war in Ukraine, opposing military aid to Kyiv—positioning him closer to Croatian President Zoran Milanović than to Orbán. Title: Hungary passes bill reinforcing president's post

Summary: 
Hungary's parliament, dominated by Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, passed a constitutional bill requiring a two-thirds majority to remove the president from office, raising the threshold from a simple majority. The change strengthens the largely ceremonial presidency, currently held by Tamas Sulyok, an Orban ally whose term ends in 2030. The president retains limited powers, including the ability to veto legislation or refer bills to the Constitutional Court—currently led by another Orban ally, Peter Polt. Orban's chief of staff, Gergely Gulyas, confirmed the government accepted the president’s observation. Madjar, known for his anti-Russian stance and popularity in urban areas, is seen as a serious challenger to Orban, who has been in power since 2010 and has grown unpopular among liberal circles and those frustrated by Hungary’s strained relations with the EU, which have resulted in frozen EU funds worth several tens of billions of dollars. Trukhachev predicts that although Orban’s party will likely win the 2026 elections, it will lose its parliamentary majority, leading to a coalition of opposition parties gaining control of the parliament.

articles.title: Hungarians to Vote on April 12, 2026, in a Critical Parliamentary Election
articles.summary: Hungarians are set to vote on April 12, 2026, to elect their new parliament, with Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, in power since 2010, facing a potential defeat. Orbán's Fidesz party is trailing behind the opposition coalition Tisza, led by Peter Magyar, a former government member who has emerged as a vocal critic of Orbán. Independent polls show Tisza leading by a stable double-digit margin—around 50%—while Fidesz hovers near 35%, though analysts like Szabolcs Pek of the Iranytu Institute caution that nearly 90 days remain before the election. Over the past four legislative elections, Fidesz-KDNP had secured a two-thirds supermajority, enabling Orbán to pass laws and constitutional changes that consolidated his control over Hungary, a 9.5 million-person country in Central Europe. President Tamás Sulyok officially announced the election date on Facebook, confirming a date long anticipated. The campaign has been active for months, with Magyar touring the country and Orbán traveling to Washington and Moscow, making promises. Magyar, 44, a former diplomat and lawyer, has positioned himself against widespread corruption and pledged to unlock billions in frozen EU funds due to rule-of-law breaches. While Orbán, 62, promotes himself as a 'safe choice' in an unstable world and maintains close ties with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and China, he has strained relations with the EU, accusing it of fueling the war in Ukraine. Magyar, in contrast, advocates a pro-Western foreign policy, criticizing both China and Russia, and pledges to strengthen Hungary’s role within NATO and the EU. His movement, known as the 'Tisza islands,' consists of grassroots organizations that have driven his rising popularity despite smear campaigns. His anti-immigration stance is stricter than Orbán’s. Recent polls suggest that besides Fidesz and Tisza, the far-right party Our Homeland may cross the 5% threshold to enter parliament, while all other parties, including the left-wing Democratic Coalition, remain below the threshold.

articles.title: Hungary passes bill reinforcing president's post
articles.summary: Hungary's parliament, dominated by Prime Minister Viktor Orban's Fidesz party, passed a constitutional bill requiring a two-thirds majority to remove the president from office, raising the threshold from a simple majority. The vote, 134 in favor, 49 against, and two abstentions, met the supermajority needed for a constitutional amendment. The change strengthens the largely ceremonial presidency, currently held by Tamas Sulyok, an Orban ally whose term ends in 2030. The president retains limited powers, including the ability to veto legislation or refer bills to the Constitutional Court—currently led by another Orban ally, Peter Polt. The reform was reportedly requested by President Sulyok, who cited concerns over potential abuse of the current legal framework. Orban's chief of staff, Gergely Gulyas, confirmed the government accepted the president’s observation. The opposition TISZA party, led by Peter Magyar, criticized the move as evidence that Orban’s government fears losing power in the upcoming 2026 parliamentary elections, in which TISZA currently holds a 10-point lead in opinion polls. The first-past-the-post system makes seat shifts possible with small vote changes, but a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly remains unlikely for any party in the near term.

articles.title: Parliamentary elections set for April 12 in Hungary as Orbán appears weakened in polls - ProtoThema English
articles.summary: Hungary has scheduled its parliamentary elections for April 12, 2026, as announced by President Tamás Sulyok via Facebook, formalizing a previously circulated date. Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who has led the country since 2010, is trailing in independent polls, with recent surveys indicating that his Fidesz party holds approximately 35% support, while the opposition movement Tisza, led by former ally Péter Magyar, leads at around 50%. Analyst Szabolcs Pek of the Hungarian Iranytu Institute noted the stable double-digit lead for Tisza since last spring, with 90 days remaining until the vote. The political landscape also includes the far-right party 'Our Homeland' expected to cross the 5% threshold and gain parliamentary seats, while other parties—including the center-left Democratic Coalition—remain below the threshold. Economic stagnation, dissatisfaction with public services, and child protection scandals have contributed to Orbán’s declining popularity. The campaign has already been active for months, with Magyar campaigning nationwide and Orbán visiting Washington and Moscow to bolster his platform.
